title: Reflex certainty of already-received grace: Reformed secondary act; Rome allows sure fiducia
source_text: LIX. Licet autem plerique ex Theologis Reformatis misericordiam illam specialem antecedentem non faciant objectum fidei respectu actus illius primarii atque praecipui per quem remissionem peccatorum consequimur, constanter tamen docent fidem justificantem circa illam versari actu quodam reflexo atque secundario, hoc est, illum qui fide justificatus est, per actum fidei reflexum certum esse posse de gratia quam est a Deo consecuturus. Quod negant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae. Sed si negent fideles & justos de impetrata a Deo remissione peccatorum suorum per fidem certos esse posse, concedunt tamen illos de ista remissione fiduciam posse concipere, & quidem ita certam, ut pellat ex animo dubitationem atque anxietatem, quod a Protestantium sententia vix differt. Adde quod non desunt in Schola Romana qui persuasionem sive fiduciam illam quam homo fidelis & justus concipit de remissione peccatorum suorum, pertendant esse cujusdam fidei divinae actum, quod supra de Catharino & Vasquez ostensum est.
pass_a_gloss: Although most Reformed theologians do not make that antecedent special mercy the object of faith with respect to that primary and principal act by which we obtain remission of sins, they nevertheless constantly teach that justifying faith turns about it by a certain reflexive and secondary act — that is, that he who has been justified by faith can by a reflexive faith-act be certain of the grace he has obtained from God. Which the Doctors of the Roman Church deny. But if they deny that the faithful and just can be certain by faith of the remission of their sins obtained from God, they nevertheless concede that they can conceive trust about that remission, and indeed so certain that it drives doubt and anxiety from the mind — which scarcely differs from the Protestant view. Add that there are not wanting in the Roman school those who maintain that that persuasion or trust which a faithful and just person conceives about the remission of his sins is an act of a certain divine faith, as was shown above concerning Catharinus and Vasquez.
pass_b_english: Most Reformed make antecedent remitted-sins certainty a reflexive secondary faith-act after justification, not the primary justifying act — which Rome denies as faith.
Yet Rome allows so sure a fiducia of obtained remission that it expels doubt and anxiety, nearly Protestant; and Catharinus/Vasquez even call that persuasion an act of private divine faith.
